title: From Newton to Lagrange: the principle of stationary action
summary: Why Newton's law is awkward in curvilinear coordinates and with constraints; generalized coordinates and the Lagrangian; Hamilton's principle and the derivation of the Euler–Lagrange equations by one integration by parts; covariance under point transformations; worked examples in polar coordinates and in a cone; the non-uniqueness of L.

objectives.description: Derive the Euler–Lagrange equations from Hamilton's principle, stating where the fixed endpoints and the independence of the coordinates are used.
Prove that the Euler–Lagrange equations keep their form under an invertible point transformation, using the identities ∂Q̇/∂q̇ = ∂Q/∂q and d(∂Q/∂q)/dt = ∂Q̇/∂q.

Write the Lagrangian of a particle on a frictionless surface of revolution under gravity by eliminating the constrained coordinate, derive the equations of motion, and check units and a limiting case.
Decide which alterations of a Lagrangian (adding a total time derivative, rescaling, adding a function of q) leave the equations of motion unchanged, with proof.

preparation.description: Read Section 1.2, Newtonian Mechanics (PDF pages 1–2): the two forms of Newton's second law, inertial frames and Galilean transformations.
Read PDF page 3: polar coordinates as 'non-inertial coordinates' (Eqs. 1.1–1.2), the Lagrangian L(q, q̇, t) and the Euler–Lagrange equations (Eqs. 1.3–1.4).

Read PDF pages 4–5: Hamilton's principle (Eq. 1.5), the advantages of the Lagrangian formulation, and the proof of covariance under point transformations (Eqs. 1.6–1.13). Work through the proof with pen and paper.
Read Section 1.5, Calculus of Variations (PDF page 22, Eqs. 1.76–1.78), which supplies the integration-by-parts step the lesson uses.
Optional second account: Tong, Classical Dynamics, Section 2.1 The Principle of Least Action (reference-only; read on the author's page).

activities.title: Lecture: Hamilton's principle and the Euler–Lagrange equations
activities.instructions: Read the lesson alongside Section 1.2 of the 8.09 Chapter 1 notes. Reproduce the integration by parts in the derivation without looking, then check it. For the polar-coordinate example, verify every unit stated in the lesson.

activities.instructions: Attempt exercise 1 before asking for any hint; write the Lagrangian, both equations of motion, the circular-orbit condition, units and the flat-surface limit. Then attempt exercise 2. Submit each attempt when you believe it is complete; revise after feedback.

activities.title: Explain: what the action principle buys
activities.instructions: Write exercise 3 without the notes open, then compare with the list of advantages in Section 1.2.

activities.title: Retrieval: definitions of the unit
activities.instructions: From memory: the definition of the action; the statement of Hamilton's principle; the Euler–Lagrange equations; the two identities used in the covariance proof; the canonical momentum.

exitCheck.description: Exercise 1 accepted: Lagrangian on the paraboloid written with the constraint eliminated, both Euler–Lagrange equations derived, the circular-orbit angular velocity found and shown independent of radius, units checked, and the flat-surface limit interpreted.

commonMisconceptions.claim: The Euler–Lagrange equation for r in polar coordinates gives m r̈ = F_r.
commonMisconceptions.correction: It gives m r̈ − m r θ̇² = F_r (notes Eq. 1.16). The centripetal term is part of the acceleration in these coordinates; the notes call them 'non-inertial coordinates' for this reason.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Hamilton's principle says the action is minimised.
commonMisconceptions.correction: It says the action is stationary. For a harmonic oscillator over more than half a period the physical path is a saddle point of S; the derivation of the Euler–Lagrange equations uses only δS = 0.

commonMisconceptions.claim: The Lagrangian of a system is unique, so two different Lagrangians describe different physics.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Adding the total time derivative of any F(q, t), or multiplying by a nonzero constant, changes the action by a boundary term or a factor and leaves the equations of motion unchanged (exercise 2).

commonMisconceptions.claim: Once a constraint is used to eliminate a coordinate, the Euler–Lagrange equations can still be applied to the original, larger set of coordinates.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The derivation requires the variations δq_i to be independent. Either eliminate the constrained coordinates first, as in the cone example, or keep them and add Lagrange multipliers (unit 2).

checks.evidence: Build agent re-derived: the Euler–Lagrange equations from δS = 0 with the boundary term vanishing at fixed endpoints; the covariance identities ∂Q̇/∂q̇ = ∂Q/∂q and d(∂Q/∂q)/dt = ∂Q̇/∂q; the polar equations m r̈ − m r θ̇² = −∂V/∂r and d(m r² θ̇)/dt = −∂V/∂θ with units N and N m; the cone Lagrangian with 1 + cot²α = 1/sin²α and the α → π/2 limit; for the paraboloid exercise, θ̇² = g/a for every circular orbit, r₀ = (ℓ² a/(m² g))^{1/4}, radial oscillation frequency 2√(g/a)/√(1 + r₀²/a²).
